title: The Spirit is named with the Father and the Son, never with the angels
english: …chapter, wielding their unbridled arguments like weapons of every kind and claiming, to snatch assent: “It is written,” they say, “‘Praise the Lord, for a psalm is good; let praise be sweet to God’ (Psalm 147:1), and ‘It is good to give thanks to the Lord and to sing to your name, O Most High’ (Psalm 92:1). But nowhere, if you please, do we find, ‘Praise the Holy Spirit.’”

They must be answered like this. If you take the words you have brought forward as spoken of the Father, you throw out the Son; if as spoken of the Son, the reverse. For the Holy Spirit too both is Lord and is written as Lord, and it is not clear here of which hypostasis “Lord” is written. Consider, then, whether you have not used these texts against yourselves.

That the Holy Spirit does not sing hymns, since he is not a creature, but is hymned together with God because he is the Spirit of God, is easier to learn both from his being ranked with God and from the fact that the three youths and the sacred psalmist bid all creation by name to sing hymns, but not the Spirit of God, though the saints are accustomed to name things one by one. For if, as the heretics say, he is of a nature midway between God and the angels, and more honoured than all and higher than all, then, since he is above all a single being, they ought either to have bidden him by himself to sing hymns, or at least to have named him first and included the rest with him as a class; not, as they presumptuously guess, the very reverse.
That he is named together with the Father and the Son. And on an objection of the heretics.

Creation is not counted together with God. For what does a thing that exists in lessening have in common with him who is highest of all and beyond all excess, or a thing that came to be with him who made it? But the all-honoured Spirit, as God, is named together either with the Father and the Son, as when the Master gives the rule of baptism (Matthew 28:19), and as when the Apostle writes to the Corinthians the second time, “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Corinthians 13:14); or with one of their hypostases; or he is mentioned even on his own, as was said in the first book.

Starting from the teaching of the outcast and rejected Valentinus, who turned Manichee and, besides his other absurd fables, said in his madness that the divine Spirit was of an age with the angels, the Macedonians say: “Paul wrote to Timothy, ‘I charge you before God and the Lord Jesus Christ and the elect angels’ (1 Timothy 5:21); but he passed over the Holy Spirit in silence, having, so they claim, ranked him with the angels.” But this notion comes out of the abundance of their own heart (Matthew 12:34).

For even if at times no particular mention is made of the Holy Spirit, he is included with God the Father, since he is his Spirit by nature. That is exactly why there are times when either God the Father himself was not mentioned in words, but only in the believing mind, while the Son and the Holy Spirit were mentioned, or the reverse. Valentinus, indeed, who ought not even to be mentioned, called the sanctifying Spirit “Paraclete,” as the Master Christ too was called “Paraclete” from being called to our side; but the ministers who are sanctified he named “angels.”

Besides this, nowhere in Scripture do we find angels mentioned together with God in the work of creation, or in the rites of initiation, or in the giving of glory. But Paul wrote of the Holy Spirit’s fellowship with the Godhead to the Corinthians in his second letter: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God the Father, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit” (2 Corinthians 13:14); and elsewhere: “If there is any fellowship of the Spirit” (Philippians 2:1).

The sacred psalmist, at any rate, proclaims how the uncreated Word and the divine Spirit differ from the ministering spirits, and that they are not of the same rank as these. Rather, by these self-complete hypostases, and through them, and for their sake, as also for the sake of God the Father, and in them, the angels were created and all things are perfected and held together. He cries out in these words: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the breath of his mouth all their powers” (Psalm 33:6). For by “word” we must understand him through whom all things were made; by “breath of the mouth of the Lord,” the Holy Spirit; and by “powers of the heavens,” both their very frames and also angels, principalities, authorities and powers. And again: “Who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flaming fire” (Psalm 104:4).

The Apostle too contends with them, crying out: “We were made to drink of one Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:13). For as it is impossible for the radiance to be parted from the light, and wisdom from the wise, that is, the Son from the Father, so too the Holy Spirit cannot be parted from him whose Spirit he is, just as with us that which …

title: The Spirit shares God's names, is one, and is the water of life
english: …we breathe. So, without noticing it, by the very arguments in which they so untimely refuse to agree with us, they are going back into the unshaken house of the beginning, from which they leapt away. They make trouble for the Apostle, who on their account, in the words of his now before us, solemnly testified before the uncreated nature and the created, much as the one who said, “I have sinned against God and against men,” and “I call heaven and earth to witness this day” (Deuteronomy 4:26; Deuteronomy 30:19), and “Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth” (Isaiah 1:2).
That he shares with God, who is Spirit, and with his only-begotten Son, in the names as in the substance.

Creation has names that are not shared with the names spoken of God, just as it has a nature that is not shared. But the Holy Spirit shares in the names of God because he shares in the nature too; except that the Father alone is called “Father,” because he alone begot a hypostasis, and the Son is called “Son,” and not father of an uncreated nature, because he was truly begotten but did not beget. So Scripture names the Spirit himself as well “Lord,” as ruling over all and sharing the one kingdom with the Father and the Son; “Holy,” as holy by nature himself and as making creation holy; “Incorruptible,” “Good,” “Love,” “Wisdom,” “Understanding,” as it has also called God; “Power,” because he gives power; “Righteous,” because he makes righteous, being himself without sin; “Paraclete,” as it calls the Son too; “Fire,” because he appeared to the apostles in tongues of fire (Acts 2:3). In the same way Moses says of the Father, “Our God is a consuming fire” (Deuteronomy 4:24), and John says of the Son, “He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire” (Matthew 3:11); and there are many more such names.
That he is one and not many, as creatures are.

Creation has nothing that exists in a single hypostasis, that is, in one person. For angels and archangels are many; so are the Seraphim; the Cherubim are not some single thing; principalities and authorities are spoken of, powers and dominions and thrones; the heavens are named in the plural, and so are men and the rest of the things that were made. Even sun and moon share with the multitude of the stars both in nature and in being of fire, as the first book set out more fully. But the oracles have proclaimed to us that the Holy Spirit, as not to be counted among creation, is one and the same.
That because he is consubstantial and without beginning, he is written to be the water of life, which has proceeded from the Father’s fountain.

Creation is not written to be the water of life, for it did not have everlasting life from itself, as God has, who lives without beginning. But the Holy Spirit is praised as being this by the sacred heralds who will be mentioned in what is written below, as proceeding by nature from the immortal and naturally living fountain of the Father, not as being created. For just as we said in the first book that light does not create its own radiance but begets it, so here we say that the fountain does not create the water that comes from it, but has it proceeding from itself and consubstantial with itself. For no one is the creator of his own son or spirit; otherwise he would no longer be father, nor one who has a spirit.

Jeremiah, speaking in the person of God: “Heaven was astonished at this, and the earth shuddered at this; for my people have done two evil things. They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves broken cisterns, which will not be able to hold water” (Jeremiah 2:12-13). The prophet sets out the mystery in a hidden way. For he called God “fountain,” and the Holy Spirit “living water”: the Spirit who in the font washes away all our sins, who cannot be torn away from the nature of the spiritual fountain, as neither can the stream that flows from springs.

Isaiah likewise: “I will give water in thirst to those who walk in a waterless land; I will put my Spirit upon your seed and my blessings upon your children; and they shall spring up in the midst of water like grass, and like a willow beside running water” (Isaiah 44:3-4). This too, through hidden words, has a spiritual sense. For to those, he says, who are ignorant of baptism, and for that reason “walk in a waterless land,” “I will put my Spirit,” who is able to make the font bring them to flower again like plants that love water, and “like the tree planted by the channels of the waters, which will give its fruit in its season, and its leaf will not fall” (Psalm 1:3).

And the sacred psalmist, out of necessity making the truth of the matter somewhat hidden in his words, sings in the thirty-sixth Psalm, “For with you is the fountain of life” (Psalm 36:9), and in the hundred and forty-seventh, “He will send out his word and melt them; he will blow with his Spirit, and waters will flow” (Psalm 147:18), “making glad the great city of God” (Psalm 46:4). And this city is the whole inhabited world. For, if I may put it so, what each city is to men, this, to the Almighty, is the …

title: Living water, and the anointing with the Spirit
english: …inhabited world.

Baruch, weeping over the people who were in the land of the Chaldeans, who did not have the Holy Spirit, cries out: “What is it with you, Israel, that you are in the land of your enemies? You have grown old in a foreign land, you have been defiled with the dead, you have been counted with those in Hades. You have forsaken the fountain of wisdom. If you had walked in the way of God, you would have dwelt in peace for ever” (Baruch 3:10-13). By “fountain” he means God, and by “wisdom” the Holy Spirit.

John, giving the Son’s words to the Samaritan woman: “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water” (John 4:10). By this he means the immortal streams of the font of the Holy Spirit. For that all these things are said of the Spirit of God, the evangelist just mentioned explained in so many words. When the Saviour had said, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, out of his belly will flow rivers of living water” (John 7:37-38), he at once added, “Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive” (John 7:39).
That the Saviour was anointed with the Holy Spirit; and if the Spirit were a creature, would not the uncreated one have been anointed with his own handiwork? And that we too have his anointing.

Creation is anointed in baptism with created oil that has been made holy. The Saviour, as God, was anointed with the all-holy Spirit, who is uncreated with him, above us who are his fellows. For if the Spirit were a creature, would not the uncreated one have been anointed with his own handiwork? The witnesses are those set down below. Isaiah, speaking for the Saviour: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Isaiah 61:1). And David: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows” (Psalm 45:7). What is this “therefore”? Because, being God not made with hands, he was anointed by God, uncreated and without beginning. And he said “your God” because of his birth from a virgin.

Peter in the Acts: “You know the word that went out through all Judea and Samaria, beginning from Galilee after the baptism which John preached: Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power” (Acts 10:37-38). The Acts again: “They were gathered together in truth in this city against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed” (Acts 4:27).

The Song too speaks of this, in these words: “Your name is ointment poured out; therefore the maidens have loved you” (Song of Songs 1:3). It says that Christ bears the name of “ointment,” the name of the Paraclete, since both hypostases share the name, and in themselves give off the fragrance of the nature of God the Father. By “maidens” it means the churches in which he is glorified. Of them David too spoke in the sixty-eighth Psalm: “Rulers went in front, close behind those singing psalms, in the midst of maidens playing timbrels” (Psalm 68:25). He put it so because their faith is proclaimed far and wide, and because they ring out into all the earth with their readings and their singing of psalms.

And in the Song the Bridegroom himself, fair in his beauty, speaks chastely to each of them: “Behold, you are fair, my companion; behold, you are fair” (Song of Songs 1:15; Song of Songs 4:1). And again he sings, as it were, a wedding song: “Come from Lebanon, bride, come from Lebanon; you shall come and pass on from the beginning of faith” (Song of Songs 4:8 LXX).

That we too receive an anointing in our renewal, John writes in his first letter: “And you have an anointing from the Holy One, and you know all things” (1 John 2:20). As the Saviour was anointed in his saving dispensation, he says, so “you too have an anointing from the Holy” Spirit.

And that this saving gift has been furnished to us by the blessed Trinity in common, they teach as follows. Isaiah: “And the Lord of hosts will make for all the nations on this mountain: they shall drink wine, they shall be anointed with ointment on this mountain. Hand on all these things to the nations” (Isaiah 25:6-7 LXX). For by “mountain” he foretold the Church of God, because of the loftiness of the faith; by “wine,” the Lord’s saving blood; by “ointment,” the oil with which, once made holy, we are anointed by the priest. John, in the same first letter, about Christ: “And as for you, the anointing which you received from him abides in you, and you have no need that anyone should teach you; but as his anointing teaches you about all things” (1 John 2:27). And Paul in the second letter to the Corinthians: “Now he who establishes us with you in Christ, and has anointed us, is God, who has also sealed us and given the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts” (2 Corinthians 1:21-22).
